revisionist

/rih-VIZH-uh-nist/ - the stress falls on VIZH · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Revisionist means favoring a reinterpretation of the accepted account of historical events.

The museum's new wing takes a revisionist line on the canal's construction, crediting the immigrant crews the opening-day speeches never named.

Example

For a century, the shipwreck was pilot error; every plaque on the seafront said so. The new book is openly revisionist: it re-dates the storm logs, re-reads the inquest, and argues the company doctored the captain's record to dodge a payout. Even historians who bristle at the book concede the inquest now reads differently.

Revisionist describes a stance toward the accepted account: it argues the standard story should be rewritten. The word cuts both ways — a revisionist case can restore a buried truth or varnish an ugly one — so weigh the evidence offered, not the label alone.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

contrarian: Contrarian describes a reflex: taking the opposite side of received opinion on principle, whatever the subject. Revisionist is narrower and more serious — it favors reinterpreting the accepted account of historical events, and it has to argue from the record. A contrarian needs only an opposing stance; a revisionist needs a rival reading of the evidence.

iconoclastic: Iconoclastic means attacking cherished beliefs and traditions — the target is whatever people hold sacred, and the pleasure is in the toppling. Revisionist aims at one specific thing: the accepted account of past events, which it argues should be rewritten. An iconoclastic essay may smash idols everywhere; a revisionist one re-argues the historical record.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

traditional: keeping to the account as it has been handed down

by-the-book: following the accepted version without question

Where it sits · how far the accepted story is overturned

questioning → revisionist → conspiratorial

questioning vs. revisionist: Questioning is milder than revisionist — a questioning historian doubts pieces of the record without yet offering a rival story.

conspiratorial vs. revisionist: Conspiratorial goes further than revisionist: a revisionist account reinterprets the evidence, while a conspiratorial one discards it in favor of hidden plots.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-: again (Latin)

Root — vis-: to see (Latin videre, visus)

Suffix — -ion: noun: the act of

Suffix — -ist: one who favors or practices

Put it together: Re- (again) + vis- (see) + -ion + -ist = one who favors seeing it again. A revision is literally a second look; the revisionist insists the past deserves one — and that the first look got it wrong.

Use the root in a new word: supervise: A foreman supervises the night pour, walking the forms with a flashlight.

Root Check

Word Choice

academic / charged

Revisionist is powerful because it is not automatically an insult: historians wear it proudly and hurl it angrily. Use it for arguments that would rewrite the accepted account; use romanticized for glow without argument, and traditional for the account being challenged.
